title: Perforated diverticulitis: Hinchey stage and choice of operation

header.contentArea: Emergency general surgery: complicated diverticular disease

related.why: General approach to the perforated viscus and peritonitis
Consenting for emergency laparotomy and a possible stoma
Counselling the patient about the stoma afterwards

brief.scenario: Mr Tom Robertson, 68, has had left iliac fossa pain for three days. Today the pain is generalised and his abdomen is rigid. Heart rate 112, BP 104/68, temperature 38.4 °C. A contrast CT shows sigmoid diverticulitis with free gas and free fluid throughout the abdomen.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on the initial management, the Hinchey classification and the choice of operation.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Septic, peritonitic patient: resuscitate, stage, then match the operation to his physiology.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Debating lavage versus anastomosis before he is resuscitated and in theatre.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "This is perforated diverticulitis with generalised peritonitis and sepsis. I'd start resuscitation and call my registrar."

grid.label: Resuscitate and escalate
grid.fail: Discusses the operation before resuscitation, or plans antibiotics and review only.
grid.pass: ABCDE; sepsis bundle: oxygen, IV fluids, cultures, IV antibiotics, lactate, catheter; nil by mouth; registrar, consultant and anaesthetist; book theatre.
grid.high: Adds a mortality risk score, a critical care bed, and consent that covers a stoma and the risk of dying.

grid.label: Hinchey classification
grid.fail: Cannot give the stages, or swaps III and IV.
grid.pass: I pericolic abscess; II pelvic or distant abscess; III purulent peritonitis; IV faecal peritonitis.
grid.high: Knows the modified version (0 mild, Ia phlegmon, Ib pericolic abscess) and that III versus IV is often confirmed only at operation.

grid.label: Match treatment to stage
grid.fail: Operates on every stage, or treats generalised peritonitis with antibiotics alone.
grid.pass: Stages I–II: IV antibiotics; abscess over 3 cm: percutaneous drainage if feasible. Perforation with generalised peritonitis: emergency surgery.
grid.high: Abscess under 3 cm: antibiotics, step down to oral; re-image if not improving. Contrast CT within 24 hours of admission if markers raised.

grid.label: Options at operation
grid.fail: Knows only Hartmann's, or offers lavage for faecal peritonitis.
grid.pass: Hartmann's; resection with primary anastomosis, with or without a defunctioning ileostomy; laparoscopic lavage for purulent peritonitis only.
grid.high: Quotes NICE: if faecal peritonitis is found, resect; resect back to soft, uninflamed (compliant) bowel.

grid.label: Choose the operation
grid.fail: Plans primary anastomosis in a shocked patient on vasopressors.
grid.pass: Hartmann's if unstable, immunosuppressed, frail or heavily contaminated. Primary anastomosis with ileostomy if stable and fit. Weighs age, comorbidity, performance status.
grid.high: Cites LADIES: 12-month stoma-free survival 95% versus 72% favouring anastomosis, with similar morbidity and mortality in stable patients.

grid.label: Evidence on lavage
grid.fail: Calls lavage the standard of care, or unaware of the trials.
grid.pass: Lavage avoids a stoma but has more reoperations and leaves the diseased colon; discuss it with the patient as NICE allows.
grid.high: LOLA stopped early for excess events; SCANDIV: more reoperations and 4 missed cancers; DILALA: similar short-term morbidity.

grid.label: Damage control
grid.fail: Attempts a long definitive operation in a patient with worsening shock and acidosis.
grid.pass: If physiology deteriorates: limited resection, stapled ends, temporary abdominal closure, ICU, planned relook.
grid.high: Explains the aim is to control contamination and restore physiology first; anastomosis or stoma decided at relook.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd start IV antibiotics and review him in the morning to see if he settles.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Stage III is faecal peritonitis and IV is purulent.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: He has a 4 cm pelvic abscess and no peritonitis. What now?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd take him to theatre for a Hartmann's.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: At operation there is faecal peritonitis. Options?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: A laparoscopic washout would avoid a stoma.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: He is on noradrenaline. Which operation?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: A primary anastomosis, so he doesn't need a stoma.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What does the evidence say about lavage?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I think it's now the standard treatment.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: ABCDE and the sepsis bundle: oxygen, IV fluids, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, lactate and a catheter. Nil by mouth. I'd call my registrar and consultant, inform the anaesthetist and book theatre.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I pericolic abscess, II pelvic or distant abscess, III purulent peritonitis, IV faecal peritonitis.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How does the stage change treatment?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Stages I and II get IV antibiotics, with percutaneous drainage for an abscess over 3 cm. Perforation with generalised peritonitis, as here, needs emergency surgery.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What are the options at operation?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hartmann's; resection with primary anastomosis, with or without a defunctioning ileostomy; or laparoscopic lavage, but only for purulent peritonitis.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hartmann's if he's unstable, immunosuppressed, frail or grossly contaminated. If he's stable and fit, anastomosis with an ileostomy, taking account of age, comorbidity and performance status.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It avoids a stoma, but more patients need reoperation and the diseased colon stays. I'd discuss it with him, as NICE allows.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: In theatre his lactate rises and he needs more noradrenaline.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Damage control: limited resection, staple the ends, temporary closure, ICU, and a planned relook.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Sepsis bundle and theatre now. I'd calculate his mortality risk, book a critical care bed, and consent him for a stoma and a real risk of dying.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: With generalised purulent or faecal contamination he's Hinchey III or IV; we often only know which at operation. The modified version adds 0 for mild disease and splits I into Ia phlegmon and Ib pericolic abscess.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: If it had been a 2 cm pericolic abscess?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: IV antibiotics, step down to oral when possible, and re-image if he doesn't improve. NICE wants a contrast CT within 24 hours if inflammatory markers are raised.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Then lavage is off the table: NICE says resect. I'd resect back to soft, uninflamed bowel.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: In LADIES, stable Hinchey III and IV patients had better 12-month stoma-free survival with anastomosis, 95% versus 72%, with similar morbidity and mortality.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: LOLA's lavage arm stopped early for excess events. SCANDIV found more reoperations and four missed cancers. DILALA showed similar short-term morbidity. So it's an option for purulent disease, not a default.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A shocked, acidotic patient won't heal an anastomosis. Control contamination, restore physiology in ICU, then decide on anastomosis or stoma at the relook.

failures.move: Planning antibiotics and review for generalised peritonitis with sepsis.
failures.consequence: Source control is delayed and septic shock progresses.

failures.move: Primary anastomosis in a patient on vasopressors.
failures.consequence: High risk of anastomotic leak in a patient who cannot survive one.

failures.move: Lavage when faecal peritonitis is found.
failures.consequence: The perforation stays open; NICE says resect.

failures.move: Pressing on with a long operation as physiology worsens.
failures.consequence: Acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia worsen; damage control is safer.

recovery.when: You lose the order of Hinchey stages
recovery.line: Abscesses come first, near then far; peritonitis comes last, pus then faeces.
Lavage is only for purulent peritonitis in a stable patient, after discussion; faeces means resect.

knowledge.fact: Hinchey: I pericolic abscess, II pelvic or distant abscess, III purulent peritonitis, IV faecal peritonitis.
NICE: abscess over 3 cm, consider percutaneous drainage or surgery; under 3 cm, antibiotics.
NICE: perforation with generalised peritonitis, offer lavage or resection after discussing both; resect if faecal peritonitis is found.
NICE: primary anastomosis with or without stoma, or Hartmann's, taking account of age, comorbidity and performance status.
DIVERTI: at 18 months, 96% of anastomosis patients versus 65% of Hartmann's patients had stoma reversal.

recall.think: Faecal peritonitis and septic shock kill; delay to source control is the danger.
recall.say: "Perforated diverticulitis with generalised peritonitis: resuscitate and theatre."
do: Hartmann's if unstable; anastomosis if stable

numbers.meaning: abscess size above which to consider drainage
contrast CT within 24 hours of admission

recall.trap: Assuming lavage is standard, or that a primary anastomosis is safe in a shocked patient.
recall.finish: Resection (Hartmann's or anastomosis with ileostomy), or damage control if physiology fails.

sources.name: NICE NG147: Diverticular disease: diagnosis and management
sources.version: Published 27 November 2019; minor updates September 2024 and November 2025
sources.supports: Contrast CT within 24 hours (1.3.5); IV antibiotics for suspected complicated diverticulitis (1.3.10); abscess over 3 cm drainage or surgery (1.3.22) and under 3 cm oral antibiotics (1.3.24); lavage or resection for perforation with generalised peritonitis, resect if faecal (1.3.26); anastomosis or Hartmann's (1.3.27); resect to compliant bowel (1.3.28)

sources.name: Hinchey EJ, Schaal PG, Richards GK. Treatment of perforated diverticular disease of the colon. Adv Surg 1978;12:85–109
sources.supports: Original Hinchey stages: pericolic abscess, pelvic abscess, purulent peritonitis, faecal peritonitis

sources.name: Klarenbeek BR, de Korte N, van der Peet DL, Cuesta MA. Review of current classifications for diverticular disease and a translation into clinical practice. Int J Colorectal Dis 2012;27:207–14
sources.supports: Modified Hinchey classification (Wasvary et al., Am Surg 1999): 0, Ia, Ib, II, III, IV

sources.name: Lambrichts DPV, Vennix S, Musters GD, et al. Hartmann's procedure versus sigmoidectomy with primary anastomosis for perforated diverticulitis with purulent or faecal peritonitis (LADIES). Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2019;4:599–610
sources.supports: 12-month stoma-free survival 94.6% vs 71.7%; no significant difference in morbidity or mortality; haemodynamically stable, immunocompetent patients under 85

sources.name: Bridoux V, Regimbeau JM, Ouaissi M, et al. Hartmann's procedure or primary anastomosis for generalized peritonitis due to perforated diverticulitis (DIVERTI). J Am Coll Surg 2017;225:798–805
sources.supports: Stoma reversal at 18 months 96% after anastomosis vs 65% after Hartmann's; similar mortality

sources.name: Schultz JK, Yaqub S, Wallon C, et al. Laparoscopic lavage vs primary resection for acute perforated diverticulitis: the SCANDIV randomized clinical trial. JAMA 2015;314:1364–75
sources.supports: No reduction in severe complications; more reoperations after lavage; four sigmoid cancers missed with lavage

sources.name: Vennix S, Musters GD, Mulder IM, et al. Laparoscopic peritoneal lavage or sigmoidectomy for perforated diverticulitis with purulent peritonitis (Ladies trial, LOLA arm). Lancet 2015;386:1269–77
sources.supports: LOLA arm terminated early by the data and safety monitoring board for an increased event rate after lavage; lavage not superior

sources.name: Angenete E, Thornell A, Burcharth J, et al. Laparoscopic lavage is feasible and safe for the treatment of perforated diverticulitis with purulent peritonitis: the first results from the randomized controlled trial DILALA. Ann Surg 2016;263:117–22
sources.supports: Short-term morbidity and mortality after lavage similar to Hartmann's in Hinchey III

sources.name: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery (O'Connell, McCaskie, Sayers, eds)
sources.supports: Resuscitation, Hartmann's procedure and damage control laparotomy

partner.opening: Mr Robertson is in resus with the findings on your brief. How would you manage him?

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for bloods or a gas
Candidate asks about the CT in detail
reveals.finding: Free gas and fluid throughout the peritoneum; no discrete abscess; thickened sigmoid.
Type 2 diabetes, independent, no steroids or immunosuppression.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks what is found at operation
reveals.finding: Purulent fluid in all quadrants; no faecal contamination; perforation sealed.

push.question: How would you manage him right now?
push.expect: Sepsis bundle, nil by mouth, senior and anaesthetic involvement, theatre.

push.question: What is the Hinchey classification?
push.expect: I pericolic abscess, II pelvic or distant abscess, III purulent, IV faecal.

push.question: How would a 4 cm pelvic abscess without peritonitis be managed?
push.expect: IV antibiotics and percutaneous drainage if feasible.

push.question: What are the options at operation?
push.expect: Hartmann's, anastomosis with or without ileostomy, lavage for purulent only.

push.question: How would you choose between Hartmann's and anastomosis?
push.expect: Physiology, immune status, contamination, comorbidity; LADIES.

push.question: What does the evidence say about lavage?
push.expect: LOLA stopped early, SCANDIV more reoperations, DILALA similar short-term outcomes.

curveballs.prompt: What is the difference between Hinchey III and IV?
curveballs.safeAnswer: III is purulent peritonitis; IV is faecal peritonitis with an open communication to the bowel lumen.

curveballs.prompt: He is on high-dose steroids for rheumatoid arthritis.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Immunosuppressed: Hartmann's rather than anastomosis, and give steroid cover.

curveballs.prompt: His lactate rises to 7 and he is cold and coagulopathic in theatre.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Damage control: limited resection, leave in discontinuity, temporary closure, ICU, relook.

curveballs.prompt: What are the chances his Hartmann's is reversed?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Not guaranteed: in DIVERTI only 65% were reversed by 18 months, against 96% after anastomosis with ileostomy.
